# Interview pitch pack

How to *present* this project: pitches, stories, a mock case, CV lines.
`docs/INTERVIEW_GUIDE.md` and `docs/INTERVIEW_RED_TEAM.md` cover how to
*defend* it. Every number below is generated by the pipeline. Quote them
exactly, and always with their label ("model-internal estimated").

---

## 1. The 30-second version

> I built a price-recommendation engine on 4.7 million weeks of real grocery
> scanner data. It estimates how sensitive shoppers are to each product's
> price, then recommends prices inside business guardrails. The headline is
> not "AI sets prices": only 2.9% of final recommendations come from the
> model's own best price. The rules set the size of the move, the model sets
> the direction. I sized the value at $234k to $538k a year for the category,
> as a range, and designed the pilot that would measure it.

## 2. The 2-minute version (situation, complication, resolution)

**Situation.** A 93-store grocer prices cereal store by store. The question:
what price, per product, per store, per week, to earn more gross profit
without risks we can't defend?

**What I built.** A validated data pipeline on the Dominick's panel, demand
models on a strict time split (ridge beats the best naive baseline clearly),
elasticities with panel-robust standard errors and empirical-Bayes shrinkage,
then a constrained optimizer with guardrails, risk gating and reason codes.
On top: an API, a dashboard, a review workflow and a grounded LLM copilot.

**Complication.** Two things a less careful version would hide:
1. The data are observational. The retailer chose its prices, so no model
   proves what a new price would do.
2. When I audited what actually decides each price, only 2.9% came from the
   model's interior optimum. A rule that ignores demand entirely matches the
   engine within 5 cents 82.5% of the time.

**Resolution.** I describe it honestly as rule-bounded pricing with a learned
direction, and I made the uncertainty usable. The value is a range across
every demand response the data supports (+4.1% to +9.4% of category gross
profit). Traffic-driver products, the ones shoppers judge prices by, get the
most increases, and capping them at +3% gives up 22% of the estimated gain.
That is a decision for the category manager. And because I could not measure
bias on real data, I built synthetic panels with known elasticities. They
show which confounders my design removes and which it cannot (unrecorded
promotions, pricing on demand shocks). That is the argument for the
store-randomised pilot as the next step.

## 3. Three STAR stories

**A. "Tell me about a finding that changed your conclusion."**
*S:* The engine looked like ML pricing. *T:* I had to know what actually sets
each price. *A:* I attributed every one of 13,964 decisions to the
constraint that bound it, and ran a no-model rule as an ablation. *R:* Only
2.9% of decisions come from the model's optimum, and the rule matches 82.5%.
I reframed the project around that finding instead of hiding it, and it
became the headline.

**B. "Tell me about a mistake you caught."**
*S:* The first elasticity standard errors used a conventional estimator.
*T:* Panel data has correlated errors within stores and weeks. *A:* I
re-derived them with clustered errors and validated against statsmodels.
*R:* The standard errors had been too small by a median factor of 3.8. The
mean shrinkage weight fell from 0.95 to 0.78, and I published the correction
rather than replacing the old number quietly.

**C. "How do you stop a model from overclaiming?"**
*S:* Every uplift number here is scored by the model that chose the price.
*T:* Make sure nobody, including an LLM, presents it as a result. *A:* I
built a claim audit that fails the build on unsupported wording, a
cross-document number check, and for the copilot a guard that rejects any
number not returned by an engine tool. *R:* 0 unsupported claims in the
repository, and the copilot cannot invent a figure: it gets one rewrite, then
falls back to a template built from the engine's results.

## 4. Mock case: "A grocer's cereal margin is falling. What do you do?"

Structure (issue tree), and where this project supplies evidence:

1. **Is it price, cost or mix?**
   - Price: are realised prices falling (promotion depth, frequency)?
   - Cost: is acquisition cost rising faster than shelf price? (AAC proxy,
     `reports/10`)
   - Mix: is volume shifting to low-margin products or private label?
     (product roles, `reports/24`)
2. **If price: where is there room?**
   - Price sensitivity by product (shrunk elasticities, `reports/14`).
   - Which products shoppers notice (traffic drivers) vs where margin can be
     built (margin builders).
3. **How to act without breaking things**
   - Guardrails: weekly change cap, margin floor, stay near observed prices.
   - Human review for risky cases (10.4% of decisions).
4. **How to know it worked**
   - Store-randomised pilot, 12 weeks, gross profit per store-week, guardrail
     metrics (complaints, out-of-stocks, basket size) (`docs/PRICING_EXPERIMENT.md`).

Synthesis to close on: *"The fastest safe lever is a guardrailed price
move on non-traffic products, measured in a pilot. The value is plausibly
4-9% of category gross profit, and I would not promise a point estimate
before the pilot."*

## 5. CV lines (edit to your own words; claim only what you can explain line by line)

* Built an end-to-end retail pricing engine on 4.7M weeks of scanner data
  (Python, scikit-learn, statsmodels, FastAPI, Streamlit, Docker). It covers
  demand forecasting, elasticity estimation with robust inference and
  empirical-Bayes shrinkage, and constrained price optimization with risk
  gating.
* Showed through constraint attribution that guardrails, not the model, set
  97% of price magnitudes, and reframed the product as rule-bounded pricing
  with a learned direction. Sized the value at +4.1% to +9.4% of category
  gross profit as a scenario range and designed the randomised pilot to
  measure it.
* Built a tool-grounded LLM pricing copilot (tool calling, provider-agnostic) with a
  deterministic guard that rejects any number not returned by the engine,
  plus an adversarial evaluation set (causal bait, fabrication, prompt
  injection).
* Evaluated the LLM copilot on a fixed 20-question set with a small local
  model: the first run passed 8 of 20 and exposed invented product codes and
  a guard gap; after fixing the tools and the guard it passed 17 of 20 (a
  development figure on the same questions, not a held-out score), with no
  ungrounded number shown in any run.
* Re-ran the unchanged pipeline on a second product category with nothing
  re-tuned: 7 of 8 headline findings replicated, and the one that did
  not is reported as such.
* Validated the estimators on synthetic panels with known elasticities. This
  measured which confounders the design removes and how far the engine's
  self-scored uplift differs from the truth.

## 6. LinkedIn post (draft)

> I spent the last months building a retail pricing engine on real grocery
> scanner data (Dominick's, 93 stores). The most interesting result wasn't a
> model score. When I audited what actually decides each recommended price,
> the business guardrails set the size of the move 97% of the time, and the
> model mostly set the direction.
>
> So I stopped calling it "AI pricing" and built around that:
> - value as a range (+4% to +9% of category gross profit), not a point;
> - a view of which products shoppers judge prices by, and what protecting
>   them costs;
> - synthetic panels with known elasticities to measure the estimator's
>   blind spots;
> - an LLM copilot that cannot invent a number.
>
> Code, a one-command demo on synthetic data, and the full write-up: [link]

## 7. Before any interview

* Walk through every module without notes: `data/`, `features/`,
  `economics/`, `models/`, `optimization/`, `serving.py`, `copilot/`. This
  repository was built with AI coding assistants (see `docs/process/`), and a
  good interviewer will probe whether you own the reasoning. Be ready to
  re-derive the profit optimum `p* = c * e / (1 + e)` and to explain why
  `Q_hat(p0)` drops out of the argmax.
* Know the five numbers cold: 2.9% (learned-signal share), 82.5% (rule-only
  match), +4.1% to +9.4% (value range), 10.4% (review share), 22% (gain given
  up by protecting traffic drivers).
* Have one sentence for each limitation in `KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md` items 1-6.
